notes:
Task and constraints: Decide whether nums can be made non-decreasing by changing at most one element.
Idea: Track the previous effective value and detect whether a descending adjacent pair has appeared.
Technique and why it applies: On the first inversion, the code treats the previous value as lowered to nums[i] when the preceding value allows it. A second inversion immediately proves failure.
Invariant: prev is the effective value at the preceding position after the permitted repair, and modified records whether that repair has been used.
Edge cases: The code reads nums[0], so it assumes a nonempty array. It does not mutate nums; the alternative branch is commented out and is not executed.
Complexity: One pass takes O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.

Task and constraints: Construct a permutation of 1..n with exactly k distinct adjacent absolute differences.
Idea: Append the increasing prefix 1 through n-k, then alternate jumps of decreasing size k,k-1,...,1.
Technique and why it applies: Alternating the sign of each jump creates the high/low zigzag that realizes every difference from 1 through k once. The prefix contributes only difference one.
Invariant: res contains distinct values in the range 1..n, and the appended suffix has used each jump magnitude once.
Edge cases: The usual constraints require 1<=k<n. For valid inputs, the starting prefix is nonempty and the suffix adds exactly k elements.
Complexity: Constructing the output takes O(n) time and O(n) space.

Task and constraints: Produce a permutation of 1..n with exactly k distinct absolute differences between adjacent values.
Idea: Alternate taking the smallest remaining value when k is odd and the largest when k is even, reducing k until the remaining sequence is monotone.
Technique and why it applies: Alternating extremes produces adjacent differences k,k-1,...,1; after k reaches one, the remaining values continue in a single direction.
Invariant: left and right delimit unused values, and each appended value is the next extreme chosen by the current parity.
Edge cases: The method assumes the standard valid range of k. Once k is one, it continues taking left values, completing the permutation.
Complexity: Every value is appended once, so time and output space are O(n).

Task and constraints: Find the kth smallest value in an m-by-n multiplication table.
Idea: Binary-search the value range and count table entries less than or equal to each midpoint.
Technique and why it applies: In row i, values are i,2i,...,ni, so min(mid//i,n) entries do not exceed mid. The binary search finds the smallest value whose count reaches k.
Invariant: The answer lies within [L,R], and count(mid) determines whether the kth value is at or below mid.
Edge cases: The search begins at zero and ends at m*n; valid k is assumed. The snippet has tab indentation in a blank region, but the executable logic is straightforward.
Complexity: Each count costs O(m), and binary search uses O(log(mn)) iterations, giving O(m log(mn)) time and O(1) space.

Task and constraints: Maximize an integer by swapping at most two digits once.
Idea: Scan digits right to left while tracking the largest digit seen to the right, recording a beneficial swap candidate.
Technique and why it applies: When a suffix maximum exceeds the current digit, swapping it into the earlier position increases the number. Later updates retain the earliest position that can benefit and the relevant maximum index.
Invariant: max_idx identifies the largest digit in the scanned suffix, with the rightmost occurrence retained when equal digits do not trigger an update.
Edge cases: If digits are already nonincreasing, left and right remain zero and the number is unchanged. The input is nonnegative under the problem constraints.
Complexity: The digit scan and conversion take O(d) time and O(d) space for d digits.

Task and constraints: Count distinct bulb states reachable after exactly m presses of the four permitted button types.
Idea: Reduce the bulb count to at most three and return a precomputed number of reachable configurations based on n and m.
Technique and why it applies: Bulb patterns repeat with period six, and each button is an involution, so counts stabilize after a few presses. The code uses known cases for zero, one, two, or at least three presses.
Invariant: n is capped at three because later bulbs repeat the first three bulbs' behavior for the button combinations considered.
Edge cases: m=0 returns one unchanged state. The constraints require n>=1; n=0 would index before the table.
Complexity: Constant-time case selection and O(1) auxiliary space.

Task and constraints: Count distinct bulb configurations possible after m button presses.
Idea: Return the known configuration count using a small decision tree over n and m.
Technique and why it applies: For n=1 or n=2, some button effects coincide; for n>=3 the number of states depends on whether m is 1, 2, or at least 3.
Invariant: Each branch identifies the equivalence class of inputs with the same number of reachable states.
Edge cases: m=0 returns one. The order of conditions handles n=1 and n=2 before general cases, and assumes n>=1.
Complexity: The method uses O(1) time and O(1) space.

Task and constraints: Count the number of longest strictly increasing subsequences in nums.
Idea: Maintain candidate tails grouped by subsequence length and accumulate counts of smaller tails that can extend to each value.
Technique and why it applies: Binary search finds the first level whose stored tail is not less than val. A new level extends all tails in the previous level; replacing a level aggregates counts from valid smaller values.
Invariant: Each sub_list level stores value/count candidates for increasing subsequences of that length.
Edge cases: Empty input returns zero. The algorithm uses strict comparisons, so equal values do not extend an increasing subsequence.
Complexity: The implementation repeatedly builds level-tail lists and sums candidates, so its worst-case time can be O(n²), with O(n) stored candidate pairs.

Task and constraints: Return how many strictly increasing subsequences have the maximum possible length.
Idea: For each index, store the longest subsequence length ending there and the number of ways to achieve that length.
Technique and why it applies: For every earlier smaller value, a longer subsequence replaces the current state, while an equal-length predecessor adds its count. A final pass through these states totals all maximum-length subsequences.
Invariant: dp[i] is the pair [length,count] for increasing subsequences ending at nums[i].
Edge cases: Empty input is not explicitly handled; it returns zero because no iteration updates result or max_len. Equal values cannot extend a strictly increasing subsequence.
Complexity: The nested loops give O(n²) time and O(n) DP space.

Task and constraints: Find the length of the longest contiguous strictly increasing run in nums.
Idea: Start a run at every index and scan forward until the next value is not greater than the previous one.
Technique and why it applies: The inner loop counts consecutive increases and breaks at the first violation, ensuring each candidate is a contiguous run rather than a general subsequence.
Invariant: For each start index i, c is the length of the increasing run beginning at i.
Edge cases: Empty input returns zero because the outer loop does not run. Equal adjacent values break a run due to the strict > comparison.
Complexity: The nested scans can revisit elements many times, so worst-case time is O(n²), with O(1) auxiliary space.

Task and constraints: Return the maximum length of a contiguous strictly increasing subsequence.
Idea: Track the current increasing run length and update the maximum at each position.
Technique and why it applies: A value greater than its predecessor extends the current run; otherwise a new run of length one begins at that value.
Invariant: count is the length of the increasing suffix ending at the current index, and result is the largest run seen.
Edge cases: Empty input returns zero because the loop never updates result. Equal adjacent values start a new run.
Complexity: One pass takes O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.

Task and constraints: Cut down all trees in increasing height order with minimum total walking distance, avoiding blocked cells.
Idea: Sort tree heights and run BFS from the current position to each next tree.
Technique and why it applies: BFS explores four-directional grid movement in increasing distance, so the first popped target gives the shortest path to that tree. The current position advances to each tree after it is cut.
Invariant: s accumulates shortest distances to trees already processed, and (ux,uy) tracks the last reached tree.
Edge cases: If a tree is unreachable, the method returns -1. It assumes forest is nonempty and the starting cell is traversable.
Complexity: For T trees and R×C cells, repeated BFS costs O(T·R·C) time and O(R·C) distance/queue space.

Task and constraints: Find the minimum walking distance to cut trees in ascending height order.
Idea: Sort trees by height and run a fresh BFS between the current position and each target tree.
Technique and why it applies: The helper explores all traversable four-neighbor cells in layers and returns when the target is reached, giving the shortest path length. The heap processes trees in increasing height.
Invariant: start is the last tree location visited, and result is the sum of shortest path lengths for trees already cut.
Edge cases: If any target cannot be reached, the method returns -1. The code assumes a nonempty rectangular forest.
Complexity: Each tree triggers a BFS that may visit every cell, giving O(T·R·C) time and O(R·C) auxiliary space; this is marked TLE.

Task and constraints: Cut all trees in ascending height order while minimizing steps on a grid with blocked cells.
Idea: Process trees in a min-heap and use a heuristic expansion split into cells closer to the target and detour cells.
Technique and why it applies: Manhattan distance initializes min_steps. Neighbors whose direction has positive dot product toward the target go into closer; others enter detour. If closer empties, the method adds two steps and explores detours.
Invariant: lookup tracks visited cells, while min_steps is the current heuristic distance plus accumulated detour penalties.
Edge cases: An unreachable target eventually exhausts both collections and returns -1. This heuristic is not standard BFS and its distance optimality is not guaranteed, so it may return incorrect path lengths.
Complexity: Each tree can explore O(RC) cells, giving O(T·R·C) worst-case time and O(R·C) storage, plus O(T log T) tree ordering.

Task and constraints: Determine whether parentheses and asterisks can be interpreted as a valid balanced parenthesis string.
Idea: Store indices of unmatched opening parentheses, closing parentheses, and stars, then use stars to repair remaining unmatched parentheses.
Technique and why it applies: Earlier left parentheses can match later right parentheses directly. Remaining stars must occur after unmatched opens to act as closes, and before unmatched closes to act as opens.
Invariant: Each deque stores indices in increasing order, and the initial scan matches every directly compatible parenthesis pair.
Edge cases: The code uses deque without importing it in the snippet. It returns True early when all real parentheses are matched; otherwise the star indices must satisfy both ordering constraints.
Complexity: Each character is processed a constant number of times, giving O(n) time and O(n) space.

Task and constraints: Check whether a string of parentheses and stars can be interpreted as balanced parentheses.
Idea: Track the minimum and maximum possible number of unmatched opening parentheses after each character.
Technique and why it applies: '(' increases both bounds, ')' decreases both, and '*' can act as either a parenthesis or empty, widening the range. A negative upper bound means no interpretation can be valid; lower is clamped to zero.
Invariant: lower and upper bound the possible open-parenthesis counts for valid interpretations of the processed prefix.
Edge cases: The code breaks if upper becomes negative, then returns lower==0; because upper remains negative, lower cannot validly represent a complete solution in that case.
Complexity: One scan takes O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.

Task and constraints: Determine whether four card values can be combined using +, -, *, and / to obtain 24.
Idea: Recursively choose two values, replace them with each possible arithmetic result, and test the smaller list.
Technique and why it applies: Every binary arithmetic expression has a final operation combining two subexpressions, so trying every pair and operation explores possible expression trees. Division by zero is skipped and a tolerance handles floating-point results.
Invariant: At each recursion, nums contains the current multiset of intermediate values, and l is the active number of entries.
Edge cases: The recursion succeeds when one value is within 1e-6 of 24. The code mutates the list during search and restores the selected values after all operations fail.
Complexity: The search is exponential/factorial in the four inputs but small under the fixed four-card constraint; recursion space is O(1) relative to fixed input size.

Task and constraints: Decide whether the four numbers can be combined to make 24 using arithmetic operations.
Idea: Enumerate ordered pairs and apply each binary operator, recursively reducing the list by one value.
Technique and why it applies: Each expression can be represented as a tree of binary operations. Commutative operations skip duplicate pair orderings, while subtraction and division consider both orders; Fraction is imported but unused.
Invariant: next_nums contains all values except the chosen pair plus their newly computed result during the recursive call.
Edge cases: Division by zero is skipped when the denominator is zero. The base case uses a tolerance of 1e-6 for floating-point arithmetic.
Complexity: The search is exponential in the number of arithmetic combinations, but the input always has four cards; recursion depth is bounded by three operations.

Task and constraints: Check whether a string can become a palindrome by deleting at most one character.
Idea: Recursively compare the outer characters and, at the first mismatch, try deleting either endpoint.
Technique and why it applies: Matching endpoints can be discarded together without affecting palindrome feasibility. At the first mismatch, only two deletion choices are possible; after one deletion, any further mismatch fails.
Invariant: has_deleted records whether the one allowed deletion has already been used.
Edge cases: Strings of length zero or one return True. Recursive slicing allocates new strings for each call.
Complexity: At most two branches occur at the first mismatch, but repeated slicing and comparisons can make worst-case time and total allocation O(n²), with O(n) recursion depth.

Task and constraints: Determine whether s is a palindrome after deleting at most one character.
Idea: Use two pointers to find the first mismatch, then check either substring formed by skipping one of the mismatched characters.
Technique and why it applies: If outer characters match, both pointers move inward. At the first mismatch, any valid solution must delete either the left or right character, so the helper verifies both possibilities.
Invariant: Before a mismatch, the substring between left and right has matching outer pairs and needs no deletions.
Edge cases: Empty and one-character strings return True. The helper checks a substring in place using indices and does not allocate new substrings.
Complexity: The initial scan and at most two helper scans are O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.
